name: Mate with king and rook
goal: You can mate a lone king with king and rook, using your king to help and a waiting move when you need one.

intro.text: A rook on its own cannot give mate, so your king has to join in. The rook marks out a box the lone king cannot leave, your king walks up to guard the rook, and one step at a time the two of them take squares away until the enemy king is stuck on the edge of the board. Near the end you sometimes need a waiting move: a rook move that is not a check, keeps the box as it is, and simply hands the turn to your opponent.

parts.title: King and rook in the corner
parts.keyIdea: The rook shuts the king into a box, and your king guards the rook so the box can get smaller safely.
parts.text: A position from Wikibooks. You are White. Your king and rook start in the corner, and Black's king stands in the centre of the board. Before the rook can do anything useful, your pieces need to work together.

credit.source: Wikibooks, Chess/The Endgame/King and Rook vs. King

notes.text: 1.Kc2, the king to c2, heads for the centre. Later the rook will need the king close by, both to stay safe and to help give mate.
2.Kd3 comes closer again. From d3 the king guards c4, d4 and e4, squares the rook will want to use soon.

3.Ra4 puts the rook on the fourth rank, the fourth row from your side, where it controls the whole row. Black's king on d5 cannot come down the board past it. On a4 the rook is far from Black's king, so it is safe there.

Black's king stepped to e5, and 4.Rd4 slides the rook right next to it. Your king on d3 guards the rook, so it cannot be taken. Now Black's king is shut in to the right of the d-file and above the fourth rank.
The king went to f5, so 5.Re4 moves the rook to e4, still guarded by your king. The box is smaller now: the f-, g- and h-files, above the fourth rank.

parts.title: When the box cannot get smaller yet
parts.keyIdea: If moving the rook in would let the enemy king take it, walk your own king up to guard that square first.
parts.text: The same Wikibooks example, a few moves later. You are White. The rook on e6 keeps Black's king in the top two rows, on the f-, g- and h-files. The rook would like to go to f6, but Black's king on g7 would simply take it there.

credit.source: Wikibooks, Chess/The Endgame/King and Rook vs. King

notes.text: 10.Ke5 brings your king next to the rook. From e5 it guards e6, so the rook is safe if Black's king comes to f7 to attack it.
Black's king did attack the rook from f7, but your king defends it. 11.Kf5 steps up again: from f5 the king guards both e6 and f6.
Black's king went back to g7. With your king on f5 to guard it, 12.Rf6 moves the rook up to f6, and Black's king is left with the g- and h-files on the top two rows.

Black's king went to h7, and 13.Rg6 moves the rook in again, guarded by your king on f5. The only square left for Black's king is h8: it is stuck on the edge, and the mate is close. It still has that square, so this is not stalemate.

parts.title: A king on the edge
parts.keyIdea: When the lone king has one square left, a rook move that is not a check can hand over the turn and force it onto that square.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's king is on the edge, on e8, and your rook on d5 keeps it off the d-file. There is no mate this move. Look at where Black's king could go if it were Black's turn.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: 90.Rd6 is a waiting move. The rook stays on the d-file, so nothing changes for Black's king, but now Black has to move, and the only square left is f8, facing your king on f6. Any rook move along the d-file that stays out of the king's reach would do the same job.
91.Rd8# checks along the back rank, the row Black's king started on, and your king on f6 guards e7, f7 and g7. Black's king has nowhere to go: checkmate.
